original_question: Does there exist a sequence x for which the range of the cardinality function F_x contains an unbounded sequence of natural numbers but contains neither omega nor c?
target_in_paper: Problem 30 in Section 6 (Cardinal function): Does there exist a sequence x such that the range of F_x contains an unbounded sequence of natural numbers but neither ω nor c? ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.17285))
correct_elements: Your draft already identifies the exact open problem the paper isolates as Problem 30, and it captures the essential phenomenon correctly: the range of the cardinality function should realize arbitrarily large finite values while avoiding the infinite-cardinality values ω and c. It is therefore very close to the paper’s official formulation. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.17285))
missing_details: The paper assumes x is an absolutely convergent real series x=(x_n), equivalently Σ_{n=1}^∞ |x_n|<∞. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.17285))
The cardinality function must be defined from the map f_x:{0,1}^N→R given by f_x((ε_n))=Σ_{n=1}^∞ ε_n x_n, with F_x(t)=card(f_x^{-1}(t)). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.17285))
It should be explicit that F_x is a function on R, so its range means {F_x(t): t∈R}. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.17285))

The paper places all possible values of F_x inside {0,1,2,…,ω,c}; this ambient codomain is implicit in your draft and should be stated for a stand-alone formulation. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.17285))
ω denotes countable infinity and c denotes the cardinality of the continuum. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.17285))

The phrase “contains an unbounded sequence of natural numbers” should be read as “attains arbitrarily large finite cardinalities”; this is the intended meaning in the surrounding bounded/unbounded discussion. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.17285))
refined_question: Does there exist an absolutely convergent real sequence x=(x_n) such that, if f_x:{0,1}^N→R is defined by f_x((ε_n))=Σ_{n=1}^∞ ε_n x_n and F_x(t)=card(f_x^{-1}(t)), then the range of F_x contains an unbounded sequence of natural numbers but contains neither ω nor c? ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.17285))
justification: Section 6 first defines the cardinality function F_x for an absolutely convergent real series and records the nearby facts that motivate the question: under one hypothesis F_x is bounded, while under a stronger hypothesis F_x is unbounded and some fiber has size ω or c. Immediately after the broader range-classification question (Problem 29), the paper singles out your draft almost verbatim as Problem 30. So the nearest paper-faithful target is exactly Problem 30, with the definition of F_x and the absolute-convergence assumption made explicit. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.17285))
